requirement: During repository validation, Habeas MUST parse every first-party Rust source file in the project: every `.rs` file except those under `.git` or `target` directories at any depth or under the project-root `book`, `evidence`, or `vendor` directories. Every explicitly declared function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, and every struct, enum, and union MUST have a valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference to a defined requirement or named example in a Rust comment attached to it or within its body. Comments belong to items under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`; a comment before a field, variant, or attribute inside an item belongs to that item. A named example MUST reference a requirement under {cite}`requirements.examples.definition`. A reference in a string literal, on an enclosing module or impl block, or only in an evidence input MUST NOT count for the items it encloses. Habeas MUST report every unreferenced item with its file, line, kind, and name, and MUST report a Rust parse failure instead of silently skipping the file.
rationale:
**Verdict:** the implementation is nearly complete and well tested, but it does not enforce one stated obligation. The requirement says a cited named example must reference a requirement. That check is missing, and no test covers it.

**What is implemented correctly**
- `rust_files` (src/rust_coverage.rs) walks the project. It skips `.git` and `target` at any depth, and `book`, `evidence` and `vendor` only when they sit directly under the root. It reports unreadable directories and entries as errors.
- `validate_rust_functions` reads each file and reports a read failure or a parse failure as an error ("cannot parse Rust source"). It also feeds those into `discovery_errors`, so a file is never silently skipped.
- `missing_function_references` parses each file with the outline `RUST_PROFILE`. Only `fn`, `struct`, `enum` and `union` nodes are checked, so methods, trait signatures, test helpers and nested functions are covered.
  - A comment counts for its node only through the outline comment-ownership rules in `src/outline/mod.rs` (`assign_comments`, `run_owner`, `trailing_owner`). Those rules give the intended behaviour: inner doc comments bind to their container, trailing comments stay with their own line, and comments before fields, variants and attributes belong to the enclosing item.
  - References in string literals therefore never count, because comments come from the tree-sitter grammar. A reference on an enclosing `mod` or `impl` does not count for the items inside it.
  - Reports have the form `file:line: kind name has no requirement or example citation`, which gives file, line, kind and name.
- `inspect_repository_with_progress` calls this check, and the call is marked `{impl}`.

**Tests**
- Tests in src/rust_coverage.rs cover most of the design space:
  - Enclosing-block references, string-literal references, unknown names, and body references.
  - Comments across a blank line, trailing comments, inner doc comments, outer doc comments, and trait methods.
  - Nested functions and test helpers.
  - Unicode text before an item.
  - Structs, enums and unions, with references attached, in the body, before a field, or before an attribute.
  - Directory exclusions at root and nested, and parse failures.
- Integration tests in tests/authoring_batch.rs and tests/commands.rs check that the findings surface in the CLI.

**Gap**
- The requirement says an item needs a valid reference to a defined requirement or a named example, and that "A named example MUST reference a requirement" (`requirements.examples.definition`). `missing_function_references` accepts any non-term definition. It never checks that a cited example itself has a `{cite}` or `{test}` of a requirement.
- `collect_definitions` does report that missing reference as an error on the example itself, and it still inserts the example into `definitions`. So a Rust item citing such an invalid example is treated as covered and is not reported.
- The test fixture `definitions()` gives `requirements.case` a `{cite}` to a requirement, which suggests this condition was intended. But the implementation never reads the example's text here, and no test uses an example without a requirement citation.

No FIXME comments acknowledge this gap, so the determination is false rather than FIXME.

Each documented profile defines which grammar nodes are comments; the Markdown
profile's comments are HTML comment blocks, so an inline HTML comment within a
paragraph is text of its section. In every supported language, comments on consecutive lines with no other source
between them MUST form one comment run. A comment that follows other source on
the same line, including another comment, MUST form a run by itself and MUST belong to the innermost outline node
containing that line. Any other run MUST belong to the next outline node that
starts after it within the smallest node containing it; when that container has
no such node, the run MUST belong to the container, which is the root node at top
level. A profile MAY bind a comment kind to its container
instead: such a run MUST belong to the smallest node containing it. The Rust
profile MUST bind inner doc comments (`//!`, `/*!`) to their container, so a
file-level inner doc comment belongs to the root node. A reference in a comment MUST count for the node its run belongs to under

An mdBook chapter MAY define an example with an opening fence of at least three colons immediately followed by `{example} <name>` and a closing colon-only fence of at least the opening length. The full name MUST use the same chapter-derived namespace and valid-name rules as `{req}`. The body MUST include all Markdown between the fences, excluding surrounding whitespace, and MUST describe a concrete case with expected behavior. An example MUST contain at least one valid `{cite}` or `{test}` reference to a requirement it illustrates; `{cite}` makes the requirement an input to the example's assessment, and `{test}` makes the example an input to the requirement's assessment, under {cite}`requirements.references.targets`. An example MAY use both. An example directive inside a fenced code block MUST remain literal.
